senses.gloss:
Jyautiṣa
(‘science pertaining to light’, [astronomy and अस्त्रोलोग्य्])
------------------------------------------
Jyautiṣa—also known as Jyotiṣa or Jyotiśśāstra—has two aspects: Vedic and post-Vedic. The former is considered as a Vedāṅga, a subsidiary science of Veda, that helps in the performance of वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्.
Since yajñas or sacrifices had to be performed at certain auspicious moments, these had to be determined first. Vedāṅga ज्यौतिष was the result of such efforts.
Ārcajyautiṣa of the Ṛgveda (with 36 verses) and Yājuṣajyautiṣa of the Yajurveda (with 43 verses) are the two works available now on this subject. They are assigned to the period 1400 B. C. Lagadha is said to be the author of the latter work which also has a commentary by Somākara of South India. The verses are very terse and even the commentary does not throw much light.
An Atharvajyautiṣa also has come to light. It has 17 chapters and 162 verses. It is considered as a much later work.
According to these works on Vedāṅga ज्यौतिष, the year was solar and had 366 days. A yuga or a चक्र or a cycle of 5 such years had been accepted for purposes of calculations. These five years were known as: saṁvatsara, parivatsara, idāvatsara, anuvatsara and idvatsara.
A cycle of five years contained 1830 days and 124 fortnights (62 full-moons and 62 new-moons). This type of calculation of the year was useful in the perform-ance of the well-known Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices. Once in five years two lunar months (60 days) used to be added to the lunar year to make it equal to the solar year.
A few more points concerning Vedāṅga ज्यौतिष may now be noted:
This way of calculation probably disappeared by 100 B. C. as the post-Vedic अस्त्रोनोम्य् and almanacs developed.
Even in the earlier period it was probably not very popular.
The basis for this ज्यौतिष was the 27 nakṣatras or asterisms and not the twelve rāśis or ज़ोदिअचल् सिग्न्स्.
Vedāṅga ज्यौतिष was gradually transcended by the works of आर्यभट I (b. A. D. 476), वराहमिहिर (A. D. 580), ब्रह्मगुप्त (A. D. 628), भास्कर I (7th century A. D.), आर्यभट II (circa A. D. 950) and भास्कर II (b. A. D. 1114). This helped in the development of Hindu अस्त्रोनोम्य् and अस्त्रोलोग्य्.
Hindu अस्त्रोलोग्य् is generally known as ‘Phala ज्यौतिष’. If अस्त्रोनोम्य् deals with the physical movement of the प्लनेत्स् and the स्तर्स् that are seen directly by the eye, अस्त्रोलोग्य् (the phala-ज्यौतिष part of the science of luminary cosmic objects) deals with the unseen results and effects they have on our lives, to be experienced in course of time.
The most important basis for this phala-ज्यौतिष or Hindu अस्त्रोलोग्य् is the belief that the स्तर्स् and the प्लनेत्स् at the time of birth of a child, have a profound influence on its life, determining the duration of its life, general condition of its body and psyche, important events in its life and so on.
This is determined by mapping the janmarāśi (the राशि or zodiacal sign based on the नक्षत्र or asterism at the time of birth) and the janmalagna (the राशि in the eastern horizon at the time of sunrise, on the day of birth).
The zodiac comprises the 12 rāśis (from Meṣa, or Aries to Mīna or Pisces) in which the 27 nakṣatras or asterisms (from अश्विनी to Revatī) are distributed.
Each one of the seven प्लनेत्स्, the two nodal points (designated as राहु and केतु) and the twenty-seven asterisms, has its own effect—good or bad—on the human being, depending upon the janmarāśi and the janmakuṇḍali. The problem, however, is in interpreting their combined effect at a given point of time, which depends not only on the astrological calculations, but also on a certain degree of intuition.
Hence, determining and predicting the future is the most difficult part of Hindu अस्त्रोलोग्य्. About 40 methods have been projected out of which the one known as ‘Viṁśottaripaddhati’ has been more widely accepted, mostly in South India. The Aṣṭottaripaddhati is more common in the North.
Based on the Vedāṅga ज्यौतिष, the ‘siddhāntas,’ secondary works on Hindu अस्त्रोनोम्य् and अस्त्रोलोग्य्, came into being in the later period. Works of आर्यभट, वराहमिहिर and भास्कराचार्य belong to this group. These works have their commentaries—generally known as ‘kārikās’—further amplifying the subject.
Works of पराशर and जैमिनि, the Sūryasiddhānta (author unknown), वराहमिहिर’s Pañcasiddhāntikā, Bṛhat-saṁhitā and Bṛhajjātaka are considered the most important works of Hindu अस्त्रोलोग्य्.
Another interesting aspect of Hindu अस्त्रोलोग्य् is the praśnaśāstra or the science of answering questions. Here, a होरोस्चोपे is cast for the time the question is asked and the results predicted, based on it.
Some findings from Greek अस्त्रोलोग्य् seem to have been borrowed by the Hindu authors of astrological works, though most of the development was indigenous.
